content: The 2019 Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), provide comprehensive recommendations and examples of effective HIV testing strategies implemented globally. These guidelines aim to enhance the reach and impact of HIV testing services (HTS) by addressing gaps in diagnosis and linking individuals to care and prevention services. The guidelines include a series of web annexes, such as Annex K, which highlights real-world examples of HIV testing programs in diverse settings and populations. The guidelines emphasize the importance of demand creation to increase the uptake of HIV testing services, particularly among populations at high risk of HIV who remain undiagnosed. Evidence-based strategies for demand creation include peer-led interventions, digital platforms (e.g., short videos promoting testing), and targeted messaging during counseling sessions. However, approaches such as personal invitation letters, general text messages, and relationship-focused counseling have shown limited effectiveness in increasing demand. Incentives have been found to boost testing uptake, but their use requires careful consideration of sustainability, equity, and long-term behavioral impacts. The guidelines also recommend provider-assisted referral (index testing) as a voluntary and comprehensive approach for people living with HIV to notify and test their partners. Additionally, social network-based approaches are suggested as an optional strategy for key populations, offering an innovative way to expand testing coverage. To support the development of these guidelines, WHO collected 57 case examples from March to July 2019, showcasing diverse HIV testing interventions. These examples were reviewed and scored by experts, with 40 high-scoring cases selected for inclusion. The case studies represent a variety of settings, including community-based and facility-based programs, and focus on themes such as demand creation, partner services, social network-based approaches, service integration, and quality assurance. Examples of successful programs include: 1. Bangkok, Thailand: A peer-driven recruitment model targeting adolescents aged 14–19 years, using the reach, recruit, test, treat, retain (RRTTR) paradigm. This program provided confidential HIV counseling and testing, along with linkage to care and prevention services. Participants received structured intervention sessions and patient navigation support, resulting in increased testing uptake and retention in care. 2. Myanmar: The Asian Harm Reduction Network (AHRN) implemented community-facilitated HIV testing services for people who inject drugs in rural and conflict-affected areas. This approach included mobile testing teams, harm reduction education, and linkage to care. The program significantly increased the number of individuals accessing testing and treatment services. 3. Mozambique: A mobile testing initiative in Zambézia Province targeted men in workplaces and social settings. The program successfully reached men who had never been tested before, linking a high proportion of HIV-positive individuals to care and treatment. The approach has since been expanded to other provinces. These case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of tailored HIV testing strategies in reaching underserved populations and improving health outcomes. The guidelines underscore the importance of evidence-based interventions, community engagement, and strategic partnerships to achieve global HIV testing and treatment goals.
